Juvenile Chaetodon melapterus recruit to coral reefs after a pelagic larval duration that typically unfolds at sea temperatures near 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. Upon hatching, the lecithotrophic prolarvae emerge from fertilised eggs measuring approximately 0.75 millimetres in diameter, a size that yields a calculated wet weight at birth of about 0.00023 grams [Wwb = about 0.00023 grams]. This initial mass is quite modest, even by the standards of chaetodontids, and likely reflects the relatively small egg size characteristic of broadcast-spawning butterflyfishes. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves for roughly the first week of life; field-based observations indicate that eclosion and the subsequent transition to exogenous feeding occur after an incubation period of approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] when water temperatures are maintained at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. This short embryonic phase is consistent with the rapid developmental rates typical of tropical marine teleosts that spawn in warm, stable thermal environments. The age at birth thus represents a critical juncture, as the newly emerged larva must quickly locate suitable prey items to avoid the point of no return.

As the post-settlement juvenile begins its benthic existence on the coral matrix, somatic growth proceeds steadily until the individual approaches the size at which gonadal recrudescence is first initiated. Morphometric surveys of Chaetodon melapterus across the Arabian Gulf indicate that the total length at puberty falls at approximately 6 centimetres [Lp = approximately 6 centimetres]. Reaching this size threshold requires a sustained period of feeding on coral polyps and small benthic invertebrates, a diet that provides the energetic surplus necessary for both structural growth and the onset of gametogenesis. This body mass is attained during the sub-adult phase, after the fish has undergone the morphological transformations associated with the larval-juvenile transition and has successfully recruited to its adult habitat. The relatively low weight at which maturation begins suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises early reproductive output, a pattern observed in several other small-bodied chaetodontids inhabiting the same region.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) provides a metric of relative gonad mass in sexually mature female Chaetodon melapterus. At a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], the GSI was approximately 6% [GSI = approximately 6%] during the peak spawning season. This value is comparable to those reported for other iteroparous coral reef fishes that engage in multiple spawning events within a single annual cycle. The index tends to fluctuate seasonally, rising sharply just before the spawning period and declining rapidly after gamete release. Such patterns underscore the energetic demands placed on reproductively active adults and highlight the importance of adequate foraging conditions to support the repeated batch-spawning events typical of this species.

Maximum body size in Chaetodon melapterus is attained after several years of steady growth on the reef, with the ultimate total length reaching approximately 13 centimetres [Li = approximately 13 centimetres]. This asymptotic length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of about 50.3 grams [Wwi = about 50.3 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length-weight conversion formula. Individuals that achieve this size are typically several years old and occupy stable territories on well-developed coral heads, where they have access to a consistent supply of preferred coral prey. The relatively modest maximum size of this species places it among the smaller members of the genus Chaetodon, a group that spans a considerable range of adult body sizes. Attaining the ultimate length involves a deceleration of growth rate as the fish approaches its asymptotic size, a pattern characteristic of determinate growers. Reproductive output likely scales positively with body size among mature females, as larger individuals can accommodate a greater ovarian mass and produce larger clutches during each spawning event.

Lifespan estimates for Chaetodon melapterus, based on field studies of tagged individuals and otolith increment analysis conducted at ambient water temperatures of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], suggest a maximum longevity of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years]. This extended lifespan is notable for a fish of such modest body size and places this butterflyfish among the longer-lived members of its genus. The species appears to exhibit a gradual senescence pattern, with reproductive output remaining relatively high until late in life before declining in the oldest age classes. The combination of early maturation at a total length of roughly 6 centimetres and a lifespan spanning two decades implies a life-history strategy built around repeated reproductive events distributed across many breeding seasons. Such iteroparity buffers the population against occasional poor recruitment years, a common feature of coral reef fish dynamics. The persistence of older adults on the reef also contributes to the stability of social structures and territorial boundaries within local populations.
